tutorial.title: Array .map()
tutorial.descriptionContent: Learn how to use map() to modify array values.

lessons.title: Intro
lessons.interactiveContent:
If we wanted to modify each element in an array and store the result in a new array, how could we do it?

One way of doing it is to use a loop to convert values before storing them. This works, but JavaScript has an even better solution.

Make sure to pick fahrenheit.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Modify every Fahrenheit value and store the converted values in a new celsius array.

One way of doing it is to use a loop to convert values before storing them. This works, but JavaScript has an even better solution.

Make sure to pick for, followed by element, fahrenheit, -, 5/9, and finally push.

lessons.title: Calling .map on an Array
lessons.interactiveContent:
JavaScript has a handy function called .map(), which, when called on an array, allows us to modify each value and store it in a new array.

.map() follows the syntax: arrayName.map(). Let's see how we can call it on the fahrenheit array.

Make sure to pick fahrenheit followed by . and then map, (, ), ;.
lessons.hardModeContent:
JavaScript has a handy function called .map(), which, when called on an array, allows us to modify each value and store it in a new array.

Use .map() on fahrenheit to start creating the new celsius array.

Make sure to pick celsius, followed by fahrenheit, ., map, (, and finally ).

lessons.title: Passing Functions
lessons.interactiveContent:
To tell .map() how to modify each element, we need to pass a function as a parameter.

We'll later program our modifications into this function.

Make sure to pick function followed by ( and then ), {, }.
lessons.hardModeContent:
To tell .map() how to modify each element, we need to pass a function as a parameter.

Pass an empty inline function to fahrenheit.map() so its transformation can be added next.

Make sure to pick fahrenheit, followed by map, function, (, {, and finally }.

lessons.title: Parameters
lessons.interactiveContent:
Before we can modify the array values, we need to pass them to the function. We do that by adding a parameter to the inline function.

In our example, we'll call the parameter element, but any name can work.

Make sure to type element.

lessons.title: Parameters II
lessons.interactiveContent:
Adding a second parameter allows us to access each iteration's index along with the array value.

In our example, we'll call the parameter index, but any name can work.

Make sure to type index.

lessons.title: Return
lessons.interactiveContent:
In order to tell the .map() function what value to store in the new array, the inline function must return a value.

Make sure to type return.

lessons.title: Arrow functions
lessons.interactiveContent:
To simplify our syntax, we can switch the inline function with a JavaScript arrow function instead.

Make sure to pick element, followed by =>, and finally element.toUpperCase().
lessons.hardModeContent:
To simplify our syntax, we can switch the inline function with a JavaScript arrow function instead.

Use an arrow function to convert every state abbreviation in states to uppercase.

Make sure to pick states, followed by map, element, =>, and finally element.toUpperCase().

lessons.title: Calling .map on an Array II
lessons.interactiveContent:
.map() doesn't only work on integer arrays, but on other value types, like strings, as well.

Make sure to pick names.
lessons.hardModeContent:
.map() calls an inline function for each array value and stores each returned value in a new array.

It works with strings too. Use function(element) for the inline function; element receives each name.

Use return for each new value. A string's .length gives its character count.

Map each entry in names to its character count and store the resulting lengths.

Make sure to pick names, followed by map, function, element, return, and finally element.length.

lessons.title: Question: Intro
lessons.interactiveContent:
Which JavaScript function can we use to modify each element and store the results in a new array?

.map().convert()

Make sure to pick .map().
lessons.hardModeContent:
JavaScript can modify each element and store the results in a new array.

You need a new array whose values are computed from every value in an existing array. Which method fits this job?

.map().forEach().filter()

Make sure to pick .map().

lessons.title: Question: Passing Functions
lessons.interactiveContent:
What do we need to pass as a parameter to tell the .map() function how to modify each element?

A functionelement

A function.
lessons.hardModeContent:
In temperatures.map(...), what tells .map() how to transform each temperature?

A function passed to .map()The name temperaturesA pair of square brackets

A function passed to .map().

lessons.title: Question: Parameters
lessons.interactiveContent:
How can we pass the array values to the .map() inline function for modification?

By adding a parameter to the inline functionBy using bracket syntax

By adding a parameter to the inline function.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You run [4, 6].map(function(element) { return element * 2; }).

What value does element receive on the first call to the inline function?

40The whole array [4, 6]

Make sure to pick 4.

lessons.title: Question: Parameters II
lessons.interactiveContent:
What can we access by including a second parameter in .map()'s inline function?

The iteration indexThe array value

The iteration index.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A map callback already receives the current value as its first parameter. What can its second parameter provide?

The current iteration index.The next array value.The new array after mapping is finished.

The current iteration index.

lessons.title: Question: Return
lessons.interactiveContent:
What must the .map() function include to properly generate a new array of values?

A return statementSyntax to modify the array value

A return statement.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You run [3, 5].map(function(element) { return element * 2; }).

Which new array does this produce?

[6, 10][3, 5][10]

Make sure to pick [6, 10].

lessons.title: Question: Arrow functions
lessons.interactiveContent:
What type of function can we incorporate to simplify the .map() function's syntax?

An arrow functionAn inline function

An arrow function.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You replace a function callback in .map() with JavaScript's shorter callback syntax. Which function type do you use?

An arrow function.A constructor function.A function declaration outside .map().

An arrow function.

lessons.title: Question: Calling .map on an Array II
lessons.interactiveContent:
What type of array does .map() work on?

Arrays of any typeOnly string arrays

Arrays of any type.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A list contains city names rather than numbers. Can .map() still create a new list by transforming every city name?

Yes, .map() works with arrays of any value type.No, it only works with number arrays.No, it only works with string arrays.

Yes, .map() works with arrays of any value type.

lessons.title: Example: Calling .map on an Array
lessons.interactiveContent:
Call the .map() function on the values array.

Make sure to pick values, followed by ., and finally map.
lessons.hardModeContent:
An arrow function uses => between its parameter and expression. It returns the expression's value.

Use .map() to create squares by multiplying each entry in values by itself.

Make sure to pick values, followed by map, element, =>, element, and finally *.

lessons.title: Example: Passing Functions
lessons.interactiveContent:
Add an inline function within the .map() function.

Make sure to pick function followed by ( and then ), {, }.

lessons.title: Example: Parameters
lessons.interactiveContent:
Add the appropriate parameter to give the inline function access to the array values.

Make sure to type element.

lessons.title: Example: Parameters II
lessons.interactiveContent:
Add the appropriate parameters to give the inline function access to the array values and indices.

Make sure to pick element, followed by index.
lessons.hardModeContent:
The inline function's first parameter receives each value. The second receives its index, starting at 0.

Use .map() to print each flavor followed by its index, using the names in console.log.

Make sure to pick flavors, followed by map, function, element, and finally index.

lessons.title: Example: Return
lessons.interactiveContent:
Code the correct keyword so that the .map() function populates the places array.

Make sure to type return.

lessons.title: Example: Arrow functions
lessons.interactiveContent:
Code an arrow function that doubles each value within the values.map() function.

Make sure to pick element followed by => and then element, *, 2.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Use an arrow function to double each value. Multiply the value on the left by 2 on the right.

Make sure to pick values, followed by map, element, =>, element, *, and finally 2.
